analysis.one_liner: Cancels EPA's rule tightening the arsenic limit in drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill to void the new arsenic drinking-water rule died in committee without ever getting a vote, and the stricter standard stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2001, EPA finalized a rule lowering the legal limit for arsenic in public drinking water. Three weeks later, this bill would have erased that rule, leaving the older, weaker standard in place. Water systems — especially small ones relying on groundwater — would have avoided the cost of removing arsenic; people drinking that water would have kept drinking more of it. The bill was sent to the Senate environment committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Water utilities, particularly small systems in parts of the country where groundwater naturally contains arsenic, would have avoided the cost of installing treatment to meet the lower limit. Those savings would have come at the expense of the people those systems serve.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water utilities facing arsenic cleanup costs

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares void the amendments to federal drinking water regulations (40 CFR parts 9, 141, and 142) made by EPA's final rule 'Arsenic and Clarifications to Compliance and New Source Contaminants Monitoring,' published January 22, 2001.
With the rule voided, the prior drinking water regulations would remain in effect as if the amendments had never been made, sparing water systems from complying with the new requirements.

analysis.who_pays: People who get their water from public systems would continue drinking water with a higher legal arsenic level. Arsenic is a known cause of cancer, so the cost would show up as added health risk spread across millions of water customers, rather than as a bill to any single party.

drawbacks.text: The rule the bill would cancel is the federal government's arsenic standard for public drinking water, so killing it would leave the older, higher arsenic limit in place and preserve that exposure for water customers.

Voiding a final rule by statute sets aside the technical and health analysis EPA went through in setting the new limit; Congress would be overriding the standard with no replacement standard of its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The only real benefit is lower compliance costs for water systems, and those costs exist because removing arsenic from water costs money. The tradeoff is that the savings come directly out of drinking-water safety for the customers of those systems. There is no substitute protection in the bill — it simply deletes the rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate environment committee and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Domenici introduced the bill on January 31, 2001, three weeks after EPA published the arsenic rule it targeted.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
That was the last action of any kind: no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further entries in the action history through the end of the 107th Congress.
Because the bill never became law, the arsenic amendments to the drinking water regulations were not voided and remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill went nowhere, water customers kept the stricter arsenic standard. The bill's passage would have benefited water utilities facing compliance costs, but that never happened.

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to void the arsenic drinking water rule and gave introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no markup, no vote, no report before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The only support on record was the Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor; there were no votes, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.note: Voiding the arsenic rule would have spared water systems the cost of treating water to the lower limit. The savings come at the expense of their customers, who would keep drinking water with a higher legal arsenic level.

industries.industry: Arsenic removal treatment and equipment suppliers
industries.note: Compliance with the new rule would have created demand for arsenic treatment systems. The bill would have erased that market, so its interest ran alongside safer drinking water.
